title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: After an excellent dinner and a great deal of cognac at Bartnyansky's, Stepan Arkadyevitch arrived at Countess Lidia Ivanovna's only a little later than the agreed hour.

"Who else is with the countess — a Frenchman?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked the hall-porter, glancing at Alexey Alexandrovitch's familiar overcoat and at another strange, rather artless-looking coat fitted with clasps.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin and Count Bezzubov," the porter answered gravely.

"Princess Myakaya guessed right," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought as he climbed the stairs. "Curious! Still, it might be useful to get on good terms with her. She has enormous influence. A single word from her to Pomorsky and the appointment would be in the bag."

Outside it was still broad daylight, but in Countess Lidia Ivanovna's little drawing-room the blinds were down and the lamps were lit. At a round table beneath a lamp sat the countess and Alexey Alexandrovitch, talking in low voices. A short, slight, very pale and handsome man, with feminine hips, knock-kneed legs, fine glittering eyes, and long hair lying against the collar of his coat, stood at the far end of the room studying the portraits on the wall. After greeting the lady of the house and Alexey Alexandrovitch, Stepan Arkadyevitch could not keep from stealing another look at the stranger.
"Monsieur Landau!" the countess said to him, with a softness and a care that struck Oblonsky. And she made the introductions.

Landau turned quickly, came over, and with a smile laid his moist, lifeless hand in Stepan Arkadyevitch's outstretched one, then walked away again and went back to gazing at the portraits. The countess and Alexey Alexandrovitch exchanged a meaningful look.
"I'm very glad you came, especially today," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, motioning Stepan Arkadyevitch to a seat next to Karenin.

"I introduced him to you as Landau," she said quietly, glancing at the Frenchman and then immediately at Alexey Alexandrovitch, "but he is really Count Bezzubov, as you probably know. Only he doesn't care for the title."
"Yes, so I've heard," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered. "They say he made a complete cure of Countess Bezzubova."
"She was here today, poor thing!" the countess said, turning to Alexey Alexandrovitch. "This separation is dreadful for her. It's such a blow!"
"And he's definitely going?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"Yes, to Paris. He heard a voice yesterday," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said, with a glance at Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Ah, a voice!" Oblonsky repeated, feeling he must move as carefully as possible in a circle where something unusual was either happening or about to happen, and to which he had no key.
A pause followed; then Countess Lidia Ivanovna, as though coming to the main subject, turned to Oblonsky with a delicate smile.

"I have known about you for a long time, and I'm very glad to get to know you better. _Les amis de nos amis sont nos amis._ But to be a true friend, one has to enter into the spiritual condition of one's friend, and I'm afraid you are not doing that with Alexey Alexandrovitch. You see what I mean?" she said, raising her fine, thoughtful eyes.
"In part, countess, I understand Alexey Alexandrovitch's position...." Oblonsky said. Having no real idea what they were driving at, he meant to keep to vague generalities.

"The change is not in his outward position," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said sternly, her loving eyes following Alexey Alexandrovitch as he rose and walked over to Landau. "His heart has been changed, a new heart has been granted to him, and I'm afraid you don't fully grasp the change that has taken place in him."

"Well, in broad terms I can picture the change. We've always been on good terms, and now...." Stepan Arkadyevitch said, answering the countess's expression with a sympathetic glance and trying meanwhile to work out which of the two ministers she was on the closer footing with, so as to know which one to ask her to put in a word for him.

"The change that has taken place in him cannot reduce his love for his neighbors; on the contrary, that change can only deepen the love in his heart. But I'm afraid you don't follow me. Won't you have some tea?" she said, signaling with her eyes to the footman who was offering tea on a tray.
"Not quite, countess. Of course, his misfortune...."
"Yes, a misfortune that has turned into the highest happiness, the moment his heart was made new and filled to the brim with it," she said, looking at Stepan Arkadyevitch with eyes full of love.
"I really think I might ask her to speak to both of them," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought.
"Of course, countess," he said aloud, "but I imagine that changes of that kind are so private a matter that no one — not even the closest friend — likes to talk about them."
"On the contrary! We ought to speak openly and help each other."
"Yes, no doubt, but there are such differences of conviction, and besides...." Oblonsky said with a gentle smile.
"There can be no difference where it's a question of holy truth."
"Oh, no, of course, but...." Stepan Arkadyevitch broke off, embarrassed. He grasped at last that the subject was religion.
"I have a feeling he'll fall asleep any moment," Alexey Alexandrovitch murmured significantly, going over to Lidia Ivanovna.

Stepan Arkadyevitch looked over. Landau was sitting at the window, his elbow on the chair-back, his head sagging. Noticing the eyes turned on him, he raised it and gave a smile of childlike innocence.

"Pay no attention," Lidia Ivanovna said, and she lightly pushed a chair into place for Alexey Alexandrovitch. "I've noticed...." she began, when a footman came in with a letter. Lidia Ivanovna ran her eyes rapidly over the note, excused herself, dashed off a reply with extraordinary speed, handed it to the man, and came back to the table. "I've noticed," she went on, "that Moscow people, especially the men, are more indifferent to religion than anyone."
"Oh, no, countess, I'd have thought the people of Moscow had the reputation of being the steadiest in the faith," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered.
"But as far as I can tell, you yourself are unfortunately among the indifferent," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, turning to him with a weary smile.
"How can anyone be indifferent!" Lidia Ivanovna exclaimed.
"I'm not so much indifferent on that subject as waiting in suspense," Stepan Arkadyevitch said with his most disarming smile. "I hardly think the time for such questions has come for me yet."
Alexey Alexandrovitch and Lidia Ivanovna exchanged a look.

"We can never tell whether the time has come for us or not," Alexey Alexandrovitch said sternly. "We should not be thinking about whether we are ready or not. God's grace doesn't work by human reasoning: sometimes it doesn't come to those who strive for it, and comes instead to those who are unprepared, as it did to Saul."
"No, I think it won't be just yet," said Lidia Ivanovna, who had meanwhile been watching the Frenchman's movements. Landau stood up and came over to them.
"May I listen?" he asked.
"Yes, of course; I didn't want to disturb you," Lidia Ivanovna said, gazing at him tenderly. "Sit here with us."
"One only has to keep one's eyes open to let in the light," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on.
"Ah, if you knew the happiness we know, feeling His presence in our hearts at every moment!" said Countess Lidia Ivanovna with a rapturous smile.

"But a man may sometimes feel unworthy of rising to such a height," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, conscious of the hypocrisy of conceding this religious altitude, but unable to bring himself to confess his free-thinking views in front of someone who, with one word to Pomorsky, could secure him the post he so badly wanted.

"You mean that sin holds him back?" said Lidia Ivanovna. "That is a false notion. There is no sin for those who believe; their sin has been atoned for. _Pardon,_" she added, glancing at the footman, who had come in again with another letter. She read it and gave her answer aloud: "Tomorrow at the Grand Duchess's, say." "For the believer, sin is not," she went on.
"Yes, but faith without works is dead," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, fishing up the line from the catechism and clinging to his independence only by his smile.

"There — straight out of the epistle of St. James," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to Lidia Ivanovna, with a touch of reproach in his voice. It was clearly a topic they had been over more than once. "What damage has been done by the false reading of that passage! Nothing keeps men back from belief more than that misreading. 'I have no works, so I cannot believe,' though that is never actually said. The very opposite is what is said."

"Striving toward God, saving one's soul by fasting," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna with a kind of disgusted contempt, "those are the crude ideas of our monks.... And yet that is nowhere stated. It's far simpler and easier than that," she added, looking at Oblonsky with the same encouraging smile she used at court to put nervous young maids of honor at their ease in unfamiliar surroundings.
"We are saved by Christ, who suffered for us. We are saved by faith," Alexey Alexandrovitch put in, with an approving glance at her.
_"Vous comprenez l'anglais?"_ Lidia Ivanovna asked, and on hearing that he did, she got up and went over to a shelf of books.

"I'd like to read him 'Safe and Happy,' or 'Under the Wing,'" she said, looking inquiringly at Karenin. And finding the book, she sat down again in her place and opened it. "It's very short. It describes the way faith can be reached, and the happiness, beyond all earthly joy, that it brings into the soul. The believer cannot be unhappy, because he is not alone. You'll see." She was just settling herself to read when the footman appeared once more. "Madame Borozdina? Tell her, tomorrow at two o'clock. Yes," she said, keeping her finger in her place in the book and gazing into space with her fine, thoughtful eyes. "That is how true faith acts. You know Marie Sanina? You've heard what happened to her? She lost her only child. She was in despair. And then what? She found this comforter, and she now thanks God for the death of her child. Such is the happiness faith brings!"

"Oh, yes, that is very...." said Stepan Arkadyevitch, glad they were finally going to read so that he could pull himself together. "No, I see I'd better not ask her anything today," he thought. "If I can just escape this without putting my foot in it!"
"It will be dull for you," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said, addressing Landau. "You don't know English, but it's short."
"Oh, I shall understand," Landau said, with the same smile, and closed his eyes. Alexey Alexandrovitch and Lidia Ivanovna exchanged meaningful looks, and the reading began.
